summary: Arabic has three numbers: singular, dual (exactly two) and plural. The dual is regular for every noun: -āni (subject) / -ayni (object, after a preposition), with ة turning into t: كِتَابَانِ, غُرْفَتَانِ. The plural comes in three kinds. Sound masculine -ūna / -īna, mostly for men described by a participle-like word (مُعَلِّمُونَ). Sound feminine -ātun / -ātin, for women and many nouns in ة (طَالِبَاتٌ, طَاوِلَاتٌ). And the broken plural — the most common kind — a new vowel pattern inside the root: كِتَاب → كُتُب, قَلَم → أَقْلَام, بَيْت → بُيُوت, رَجُل → رِجَال. Learn every noun with its plural. Plurals of things agree as feminine singular (هٰذِهِ كُتُبٌ); plurals of people take plural agreement (هٰؤُلَاءِ طُلَّابٌ).

head: pattern
plurals of the nouns you know
rows: أَقْلَام، أَبْوَاب، أَوْلَاد، أَطْفَال، أَشْخَاص، أَوْرَاق
blocks.caption: The patterns are written with the model root ف ع ل: كُتُب is فُعُل, أَقْلَام is أَفْعَال.

blocks.title: Things in the plural are “she”.
blocks.text: Any plural that is not people agrees as one feminine thing: هٰذِهِ كُتُبٌ, الْمَفَاتِيحُ؟ هِيَ هُنَا, كُتُبٌ كَثِيرَةٌ. People keep the plural: هٰؤُلَاءِ طُلَّابٌ, أَصْدِقَاءُ كَثِيرُونَ.

blocks.title: The dual is always regular.
blocks.text: Singular + -āni (subject) / -ayni (object, after prepositions): بَيْتٌ → بَيْتَانِ / بَيْتَيْنِ; ة becomes t: غُرْفَةٌ → غُرْفَتَانِ. With the article: الْكِتَابَانِ. People agree in the dual: الطَّالِبَانِ هُنَا.

blocks.title: Plurals with two endings only.
blocks.text: The sound feminine plural has -i in the accusative: رَأَيْتُ الطَّالِبَاتِ, never *الطَّالِبَاتَ. Many long broken plurals (مَفَاتِيحُ, نَوَافِذُ, حَقَائِبُ, أَصْدِقَاءُ, كَرَاسِيُّ) are diptotes: no tanwīn, and -a for both accusative and genitive when indefinite: ثَلَاثَةُ مَفَاتِيحَ.

items.title: sound plural
points: an ending on the unchanged singular
predictable once you know which one

items.title: broken plural
points: a new vowel pattern inside the root
most nouns, many people too (رِجَال, طُلَّاب)
learn it with the noun, like a German plural

blocks.text: Collective nouns are a fourth group: وَرَق (paper, the material) is grammatically singular; one sheet is the unit noun وَرَقَة, and sheets are أَوْرَاق. Many fruits and vegetables work the same way (later lessons).

askYourself: Exactly two? → the dual: -āni (subject) / -ayni (object, after a preposition); ة becomes t.
A man or men described by a participle-like word (مُعَلِّم)? → maybe the sound masculine -ūna / -īna — check the word.
A woman (طَالِبَة) or a noun in ة (طَاوِلَة)? → often the sound feminine -āt.
Otherwise → a broken plural: learn it with the noun (كِتَاب / كُتُب).
Is the plural a thing, not people? → feminine singular agreement: هٰذِهِ، هِيَ، كَثِيرَةٌ.
Is it a long pattern (مَفَاعِيل، فَوَاعِل، فَعَائِل، أَفْعِلَاء)? → a diptote: no tanwīn (مَفَاتِيحُ).

traps: Sound feminine plural: the accusative ends in -i: الطَّاوِلَاتِ, طَاوِلَاتٍ — never *طَاوِلَاتًا.
Things in the plural are “she”: الْكُتُبُ؟ هِيَ هُنَا — not *هُمْ.
Not every masculine person noun takes -ūna: طَالِب → طُلَّاب, صَدِيق → أَصْدِقَاء, رَجُل → رِجَال.
The plural can come from another word: اِمْرَأَة → نِسَاء.
A collective is singular: الْوَرَقُ هُنَا (the paper is here).
Two of something is the dual, not the plural: كِتَابَانِ.

quiz.why: A broken plural (pattern فُعُل); كِتَابَات means “writings”.
A broken plural, even though it is a person.
Things in the plural agree as feminine singular.
The dual of the singular, ة → t, -āni for the subject.

quiz.q: Which ending can the plural طَاوِلَات NOT take?
quiz.why: The sound feminine plural has only -un and -in: the accusative is -in too.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew plurals are mostly regular (-ִים / -וֹת) with few broken ones; Hebrew also keeps a dual for some nouns (יוֹמַיִם, two days; עֵינַיִם, eyes).
German plurals also have to be learned with each noun (-e, -er, -(e)n, -s, umlaut) — the same habit as Arabic broken plurals.
Chinese nouns have no plural: 们 is added only for people; things are counted with a number and a measure word.
After 3–10 the noun is plural, after 11–99 singular again — see the numbers.

notes.text: Greek plurals change the ending (βιβλίο → βιβλία); Arabic most often changes the inside of the word (كِتَاب → كُتُب), has a dual for two, and treats plurals of things as feminine singular.
Russian has unit nouns like the Arabic ones: горох → горошина (a pea), картофель → картофелина (a potato) — compare بَصَل → بَصَلَة (an onion). New are the dual and the broken plurals.
Spanish adds -s / -es to every noun; most Arabic plurals are broken — a new vowel pattern inside the word (قَلَم → أَقْلَام) — and are learned with each noun.
English has a few inside-the-word plurals (foot → feet, man → men); in Arabic that is the most common kind (رَجُل → رِجَال), and there is a dual for two.
Hindi plurals change the ending by gender (लड़का → लड़के, किताब → किताबें); Arabic often changes the inside of the word and has a dual.
Persian uses Arabic broken plurals for many Arabic loanwords (کتب, اخبار) besides its own -hā / -ān, and even the Arabic ending -āt (سبزیجات, vegetables); in Arabic these are the normal plurals.
Turkish has one plural ending, -ler / -lar, and drops it after numbers; Arabic has three kinds of plural plus a dual, learned with each noun.
Japanese nouns usually do not mark plural; Arabic must choose singular, dual or plural every time.
Finnish plurals are regular (-t, -i-); Arabic plurals are mostly broken and are learned with each noun.
Hungarian adds -k (könyvek); Arabic mostly changes the vowels inside the word (كُتُب).
Swahili makes the plural by changing the prefix (kitabu → vitabu), Arabic often by changing the vowels inside (كِتَاب → كُتُب) — in both, learn the pair.
Luganda changes the class prefix (ekitabo → ebitabo), Arabic often changes the inside of the word — in both, learn the pair.
Vietnamese marks plural only with words like các / những; Arabic marks it on the noun itself, with a dual for two.
Inuktitut also has singular, dual and plural: inuk, inuuk, inuit (one, two, several people) — like Arabic -āni for two; but Arabic plurals are often broken.
